question: A patient with Parkinson's disease on levodopa/carbidopa for 7 years reports that his PD symptoms return predictably about 3 hours after each dose, improving again with the next dose. He also describes involuntary writhing movements of his arms and trunk occurring about 60–90 minutes after each dose, at the time when he feels 'at his best'. Which complication best describes the involuntary movements he experiences at his best?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Wearing-off describes the return of parkinsonian symptoms as levodopa plasma levels fall before the next dose — this matches the first symptom described (symptoms 3 hours after dose). The involuntary movements at 'best' time are a different, separate complication.

Correct. Peak-dose dyskinesias are choreiform or dystonic involuntary movements occurring at peak levodopa plasma levels — when the patient feels most mobile. They reflect dopaminergic overstimulation of the striatum at peak drug concentrations. Management options include reducing individual levodopa doses (while increasing frequency), adding amantadine, or considering DBS.

Incorrect. Diphasic dyskinesias occur at the beginning and end of the dose effect (as levels rise and fall through a critical zone), not at peak. They are often dystonic rather than choreiform and less common than peak-dose dyskinesia.

Incorrect. Off-period dystonia is painful dystonic cramping occurring during off-periods (early morning before first dose is classic). It occurs when levodopa levels are low, not at peak effect when the patient feels well.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the motor complications of long-term levodopa: wearing-off (end-of-dose return of PD symptoms), peak-dose dyskinesia (involuntary movements at peak, when patient feels best), diphasic dyskinesia (onset and offset of dose), and off-period dystonia (painful cramping during off-periods). Timing relative to the dose cycle is the diagnostic key.

Well done. Distinguishing wearing-off from peak-dose dyskinesia is fundamental to managing advanced PD — they require opposite adjustments (wearing-off = extend coverage; peak-dose dyskinesia = reduce peak concentration). Both can coexist, as in this patient.
